blocks.prompt: Every Bee Has a Job
blocks.text: A hive is a busy town. Every bee in it has a job. The queen bee has one job. She lays the eggs. She can lay more than a thousand eggs in a day. The worker bees do everything else. Some clean the rooms. Some feed the babies. Some build walls out of wax. Some stand at the door and guard it. The oldest workers get the best job of all. They fly out to the flowers. They bring back nectar and pollen. Then the whole hive eats.

blocks.prompt: The Bee That Changes Jobs
blocks.text: A worker bee lives for about six weeks in summer, and in that short life she does almost every job in the hive. She starts on her first day by cleaning out the cell she hatched from. Nothing goes into a dirty cell. For the next week she is a nurse. She feeds the tiny white grubs, called larvae, that will become the next bees. Then her wax glands start working. She eats honey, and flakes of wax push out through her belly. She chews the flakes soft and builds them into six sided rooms. Every room is a hexagon, because hexagons fit together with no gaps and use the least wax. Later she guards the door, sniffing every bee that lands to check it belongs. Only at the end of her life does she fly out to the flowers. She has waited her whole life for the sky.

answers: she cleans out the cell she hatched from
flakes of wax push out through her belly after she eats honey
hexagons fit together with no gaps and use the least wax
(inference: flying outside is the most dangerous job, so it is saved for the end of her life)

4.title: The Bee That Dances Directions
4.subtitle: A reading and science sheet for ages 9 to 10
4.intro: Read the passage, then answer in full sentences. Some questions ask what you think, not just what the passage says.

blocks.prompt: Read the passage, then work through each part.

notes: The waggle dance is a map
Bees steer by the sun
They can see ultraviolet light
Karl von Frisch won a Nobel Prize in 1973
The whole dance happens in the dark

blocks.prompt: The Dance That Draws a Map
blocks.text: A bee finds a patch of clover half a mile from the hive. She fills up on nectar and flies home. Now she has a problem. She cannot lead the others there one by one, and she cannot point. So she dances. Inside the hive it is dark and crowded. The bee climbs onto the wall of the honeycomb and runs in a straight line, shaking her body from side to side. Then she loops back and runs the same line again, and again, tracing a shape like the number eight. Other bees crowd around her and feel the dance with their antennae. Everything they need is in that straight run. The angle of the run tells them the direction. If she runs straight up the wall, the flowers lie toward the sun. If she runs at forty degrees to the right of straight up, the flowers lie forty degrees to the right of the sun. The length of the waggle tells them the distance. A longer shake means a longer flight. A scientist named Karl von Frisch spent years watching bees through glass, marking them with tiny dots of paint, until he worked out what the dance meant. In 1973 he was given a Nobel Prize for reading it. A bee had been giving directions in the dark all along, and nobody had understood a word.

blocks.prompt: Answer each question in full sentences.
items: What problem does the bee have when she gets home, and how does she solve it?
The dance tells the other bees two things. What are they, and which part of the dance carries each one?
The other bees cannot see the dance. How do they read it?
Straight up the wall of a dark hive means toward the sun. Why is that surprising, and what does it tell you about how well bees keep track of the sun?
answers: she cannot lead them or point to the flowers, so she dances the directions
direction, from the angle of the straight run; distance, from the length of the waggle
they crowd around and feel the dance with their antennae
(inference: she is in the dark and cannot see the sun, so she must remember its position and keep updating it as it moves)

5.title: The Bee That Dances Directions
5.subtitle: A reading and science sheet for ages 11 to 12
5.intro: Read the passage, then answer in full sentences. Use evidence from the text where the question asks for it.

blocks.prompt: Read the passage, then work through each part.

notes: Nectar is about 80 percent water
Finished honey is about 17 percent water
One worker makes about 1/12 of a teaspoon in her life
Roughly two million flowers fill one jar
Capped honey keeps for years without spoiling
Enzymes in her honey stomach start the work mid flight

blocks.prompt: Two Million Flowers
blocks.text: Honey does not come out of a flower. It has to be made, and making it is one of the strangest manufacturing jobs in nature. It starts as nectar, which is mostly water with some sugar dissolved in it. A forager bee drinks nectar into a stomach she does not digest with, a stretchy pouch sometimes called a honey stomach. Flying home, enzymes in that pouch begin splitting the long sugar in nectar into two simpler sugars. Back at the hive she does not store it herself. She passes the load mouth to mouth to a younger house bee, who works it over with her tongue, exposing it to the warm air, adding more enzymes, and passing it on again. The nectar is chewed and handed around until its chemistry has changed. Then comes the drying. The house bees spread the thin syrup into wax cells and fan it with their wings, thousands of them, hour after hour, driving off water until what began as roughly eighty percent water is down to about seventeen. That is the whole trick. Honey is too sweet and too dry for mold or bacteria to live in, and it is slightly acidic besides. Sealed under a wax cap, it will keep for years without spoiling. When the water is gone, a bee caps the cell with fresh wax and the pantry is closed. The cost is enormous. A single worker bee, over her entire six week life, produces about one twelfth of a teaspoon of honey. To fill one jar, the hive must visit roughly two million flowers and fly a distance greater than the trip around the Earth. No bee ever sees the jar filled. Each one contributes a smear of sweetness to a store she is unlikely to eat, in a winter she will not live to see.

(inform, with detail: it explains a process step by step and gives numbers; the closing lines add a persuasive, emotional note)

6.title: The Bee That Dances Directions
6.subtitle: A reading and science sheet for age 13
6.intro: Read the passage closely, then answer in full sentences. Cite the text directly where a question asks for evidence.

blocks.prompt: Read the passage, then work through each part.

notes: Apis mellifera
A swarm is half a colony leaving with the old queen
Scouts dance harder for better homes
A quorum of about 15 bees ends the debate
Thomas Seeley worked this out on an island
Piping warms the flight muscles for takeoff

blocks.prompt: How a Swarm Makes Up Its Mind
blocks.text: In late spring a healthy hive does something that looks like a disaster and is actually a birth. The old queen leaves, and roughly half the colony leaves with her. Ten thousand bees pour out of the entrance, fill the air, and then settle into a hanging beard on a nearby branch. They have no home. They are carrying only the honey in their stomachs, enough for about three days. Somewhere within a few miles there is a hollow tree that will keep them alive through winter, and somewhere else there are a dozen hollows that will kill them. The swarm has to choose, and it has no leader. What happens next was worked out over decades, largely by a biologist named Thomas Seeley, who carried hives to an island with almost no natural nest sites, built wooden boxes of different sizes, and watched which ones the bees picked. A few hundred of the oldest bees leave the cluster as scouts. Each one searches alone. When a scout finds a possible home she inspects it carefully, walking the inside walls, measuring the volume by crawling around it, checking the size of the entrance and its height off the ground. Then she flies back and dances on the surface of the swarm, the same waggle dance foragers use for flowers, except that here it advertises real estate. And here is the part that matters. She dances with an enthusiasm that matches the quality of what she found. A superb cavity earns a hundred circuits of dancing. A mediocre one earns ten. A poor one earns none, because she does not bother to dance at all. Other scouts watch, fly out to inspect the advertised site themselves, and come back with their own independent opinion. They do not simply copy the dancer. A bee who visits a mediocre cavity dances weakly for it no matter how hard the first bee sold it. Good sites accumulate dancers. Bad sites lose them. Every dancer also fades, dancing a little less on each return, so a site only holds support if new bees keep confirming it. Support has to be earned again and again or it evaporates. Eventually scouts gathered at one site notice that a crowd has formed there, a quorum of perhaps fifteen or twenty bees. That threshold, not a majority vote, is the decision. The scouts race home, run through the cluster piping a high shrill signal that warms the flight muscles of ten thousand bees, and the whole swarm lifts off and flies, usually straight, to a hole in a tree that most of them have never seen. The colony has no leader, no map, and no shared language beyond a shaking body and a shrill note. It still makes the right choice almost every time. Seeley's point, put plainly, is that a group can be smarter than any of its members if it gathers many independent opinions, lets evidence rather than volume decide, and does not let the loudest scout win.

blocks.prompt: Answer in full sentences. Quote the text exactly where a question says to cite it.
items: Summarize the passage in ONE sentence without reusing any phrase from it.
Explain how a scout's dance carries information about quality, not just location. Cite the evidence.
The passage says the scouts do not simply copy the dancer. Explain why that independence is the thing that makes the system work.
Explain the difference between a quorum and a majority vote, and why the passage bothers to make that distinction. Cite the sentence that draws it.
Analyze the last sentence. What is the author doing by ending on people rather than on bees, and has the passage earned that move?
answers: (original one-sentence summary: a leaderless swarm picks a new home by having scouts inspect sites independently and advertise them in proportion to quality until enough agree)
(dance length scales with site quality; cite: A superb cavity earns a hundred circuits of dancing. A mediocre one earns ten.)
(if bees copied the dancer, an early enthusiastic scout could sell a bad site; independent inspection means the site itself, not the salesmanship, generates support)
(a quorum is a threshold of bees gathered at the site, not a count of the whole group; cite: That threshold, not a majority vote, is the decision)

(it turns a nature passage into an argument about how groups should decide; earned if the reader accepts the independence and decay evidence, arguable because bees are not people and the passage offers no human example)
